report:
I would not answer “yes.” The best current evidence says CoQ10 is generally safe but has not been shown to improve Parkinson’s movement symptoms or slow functional decline.

Why “yes” seemed plausible: a small 2002 trial reported that CoQ10 “appears to slow” deterioration, but the authors explicitly said results needed confirmation in a larger study: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12374491/

That confirmation failed. The phase III QE3 trial tested high-dose CoQ10 (1200 and 2400 mg/day) in early Parkinson’s and found it “safe and well tolerated” but with “no evidence of clinical benefit”; it was stopped after meeting a futility criterion: https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/1851409

A meta-analysis of randomized trials reached the same bottom line: CoQ10 was safe/well tolerated but “no superior to placebo” for motor symptoms: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10072-016-2757-9

So the evidence behind a “yes” is weak and outdated; the stronger, later trials are negative. CoQ10 should not replace levodopa or other proven Parkinson’s treatments, and any supplement use should be discussed with a neurologist because of cost, interactions, and false hope.
